# SVAEval: An Evaluation Framework for LLM-based SVA Property Generators

Yu-An Shih, SooHyuk Cho, Aarti Gupta and Sharad Malik Princeton University, Princeton, USA {yashih, soohyuk.cho}@princeton.edu, aartig@cs.princeton.edu, sharad@princeton.edu Artifact Available

10.5281/zenodo. 20131022

Abstract—Assertion-based verification (ABV) uses SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA) to formally specify design behavior, but constructing high-quality SVA properties remains a labor-intensive and error-prone process. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have enabled automated SVA generation from design specification documents; however, there are limitations in how the quality of the generated SVA properties, and thus the SVA generator, is evaluated. Existing automatic evaluation methods rely on formal tools – such as model checking and coverage analysis – to measure the correctness and completeness of the generated properties against a golden RTL implementation. However, it is difficult to obtain bug-free RTL designs, and even if they are available, the computed metrics do not accurately reflect the quality of generated properties against design specifications. We propose SVAEVAL, an automatic approach to evaluate SVA property generators, by directly evaluating the generated property sets without the need of golden RTL implementations. SVAEVAL considers two different scenarios: (1) If a humanexpert-generated golden SVA property set is available (e.g., in a benchmark set), a formal framework is used to accurately evaluate the quality of the generated property set against the golden set. (2) Without a golden SVA property set, a hybrid formal and LLM-based framework is used to compare the quality of two generated property sets from different SVA generators. Experimental results demonstrate that SVAEVAL provides significantly more reliable evaluation than prior approaches, and offer new insights into the capabilities and limitations of various LLM-based SVA property generators. Index Terms—Assertion-based verification (ABV), SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA), Large Language Models (LLMs), property generation, evaluation methodologies

I. INTRODUCTION

Assertion-based verification (ABV) [1] is a core methodology in modern hardware design, enabling designers to formally specify hardware properties using temporal logic. These properties, usually written in SystemVerilog Assertion (SVA) [2], specify both legal input from the environment (assumptions) and expected design behavior (assertions). These SVA properties are concurrent assertions, which are temporal properties that hold for the entire design, in contrast to immediate assertions, which hold at some point in the code. The registertransfer level (RTL) design is then verified with simulation or formal verification to ensure that all assertions pass under the assumptions.

However, developing high-quality SVA properties for industrial designs is a labor-intensive process. Verification engineers read design specification documents, identify relevant information for verification, and translate those natural language descriptions into SVA properties. This process is timeconsuming and error-prone, often requiring multiple iterations before a correct and complete property set is constructed [3]. Recent research has explored the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) to assist human engineers in generating SVA properties from natural language specifications, including sentence/paragraph-level NL-to-SVA translation [4]–[9] and end-to-end SVA generation frameworks [10]–[17]. While these approaches show promise in reducing manual effort, there is a lack of reliable evaluation methods to determine how well the generated properties reflect the intended design behavior. An SVA property set should be evaluated in various aspects: (1) correctness, ensuring that the properties are consistent with the specification; and (2) completeness: ensuring that all required design constraints in the specification are captured. An additional feature is (3) usefulness, ensuring that each property contributes to meaningful design behavior, instead of being a tautology or a redundant property. In a typical functional verification flow, both correctness and completeness gradually improve throughout the verification process. For example, when the design contradicts an assertion, verification engineers analyze the root cause and determine whether to report a hardware bug or modify the assertion. For completeness, coverage analysis tools [18] are used to identify portions in the design that are not covered by any assertions, providing hints towards adding more design constraints. Usefulness is usually implicitly guaranteed by the expertise of human engineers. Recent works on LLM-based SVA generation often rely on automatic tools to evaluate the quality of generated properties with golden, i.e., bug-free, RTL implementations [11], [13]– [16] of the design specification. For example, to measure correctness, model checkers [19] are used to formally verify the generated assertions, marking the passed assertions as correct. Coverage analysis tools are then used to compute the coverage of these passed assertions on the RTL implementation, as a measurement of completeness. A challenge for this evaluation paradigm is the difficulty in obtaining a bug-free RTL design. In academia, where

open-source RTL designs are seldom thoroughly verified, it is difficult to guarantee that an RTL implementation of a complex design specification is golden. In industry, an RTL design might not even exist during early design stages, and would not be thoroughly verified until the end of the functional verification flow. Even if a golden RTL implementation exists, this evaluation paradigm still doesn’t accurately reflect the quality of an SVA property set with respect to the design specification. For example, (i) tautologies and redundant properties will pass model checking, increasing the number of “correct” assertions without specifying meaningful design behavior; (ii) Assumptions cannot be checked by the formal tools and, if incorrect, can also make assertion checks inaccurate; (iii) An RTL design need not implement all allowed behaviors of the specification, and thus cannot check assertions that are not covered by its behavior. Detailed explanations and examples will be provided in Section II. Moreover, since it requires significant effort to manually develop SVA properties, the datasets used in recent SVA generation research often only contain specification documents without any golden property sets. Without such manually developed properties, it is impossible to evaluate the effectiveness of current SVA generators compared to human engineers. To address these issues, we put together a dataset with manually developed SVA property sets, building on existing open-source efforts that developed formal specifications for standard hardware protocols [12], [20]. With the humanexpert-generated “golden” SVA property sets, we propose SVAEVAL-FORMAL, a formal evaluation framework that rigorously evaluates the quality metrics (correctness, completeness, and usefulness) of any “test” SVA property sets. With this framework, we systematically evaluate various LLM-based SVA generators and observe limitations of current technologies that were not captured by previous evaluation methods. We consider a second scenario without golden SVA property sets. Here, we combine formal and LLM-based techniques to compare the relative correctness and completeness of different SVA generators. Specifically, formal methods are used to identify properties with which the two SVA property sets disagree, and an evaluation LLM is used to determine their correctness with respect to the document. This results in SVAEVAL-

HYBRID, an evaluation framework that can accurately compare different SVA generators without manual inspection. The contributions of our work are summarized as follows:

• We identify the limitations of RTL-implementation-based evaluation methods widely used in recent LLM-based SVA generation research, highlighting their inaccuracy in measuring the correctness, completeness, and usefulness of generated properties against specification documents.

• We propose SVAEVAL, an SVA evaluation approach that considers two different scenarios: (1) With human-expertgenerated golden SVA property sets, SVAEVAL-FORMAL formally evaluates property sets from any generators; (2) Without golden SVA property sets, SVAEVAL-HYBRID

combines formal and LLM-based techniques to compare property sets from different generators.

• Applying SVAEVAL-FORMAL to our dataset, we systematically evaluate various LLM-based SVA generation techniques, uncovering previously unreported limitations that are not captured by existing evaluation approaches.

• We assess the accuracy of SVAEVAL-HYBRID with the same dataset and show that it has an average error rate of 9.48%. This provides confidence in using SVAEVAL to compare SVA generators without manually developed golden property sets. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II describes inaccuracies of the widely used RTLimplementation-based SVA evaluation methods. Section III explains the details of SVAEVAL, including the (1) formal evaluation framework with golden SVA property sets and (2) hybrid formal and LLM-based comparison framework without golden SVA property sets. In Section IV, we evaluate various SVA generators, demonstrating that SVAEVAL is more accurate than existing RTL-implementation-based approaches in evaluating the correctness, completeness and usefulness of generated SVA property sets. In Section V, we further analyze the effectiveness of current SVA generation techniques and identify remaining challenges. Section VI highlights limitations of our methods, and Section VII discusses related work. Finally, we provide concluding remarks and indicate future directions in Section VIII.

II. RTL-IMPLEMENTATION-BASED EVALUATION

Recent research on LLM-based SVA generation relies on automatic tools to evaluate the generated properties against golden, i.e., bug-free, RTL implementations [11], [13]–[16]. However, the correctness and completeness of an SVA property set should be assessed with reference to the specification rather than to a valid implementation. This mismatch, without proper manual inspection, introduces inaccuracy regarding the quality of the generated properties. Without loss of generality, we focus on two most widely used evaluation methods in recent literature – model checking to evaluate correctness, and coverage analysis to evaluate completeness. We discuss sources of their inaccuracies and provide real-world examples. Practical experimental results demonstrating these inaccuracies are shown in Section IV-C.

A. Model Checking to Evaluate Correctness

Model checking is widely used in formal hardware verification to debug RTL designs. Given the RTL design and a set of SVA properties, it checks whether each assertion holds under the assumptions:

∀p ∈Passert, R ∧Passume |= p

where Passert and Passume denote the assertions and assumptions in the property set, and R denotes the RTL design. Numerous efforts on LLM-based SVA generation [11], [13]–[16] have adopted model checking to measure the correctness of generated properties. Assuming a golden RTL

implementation, the number/rate of passed assertions are used as a measure of correctness. We identify multiple sources of inaccuracies for this evaluation strategy, as listed below. 1) Tautologies and redundant properties: LLMs generate tautologies and redundant properties (Figs. 1 and 2). These properties pass assertion checks, increasing correctness number/rate without adding value to the entire property set. 2) Under-/Over-constrained assumption sets: Assumptions cannot be verified using an RTL design, since they are environment constraints that specify legal inputs instead of expected design behaviors. Moreover, a flawed assumption set may invalidate assertion checks. An under-constrained assumption set allows invalid inputs to the design, which may cause correct assertions to fail, resulting in false negatives. Conversely, an over-constrained assumption set may create false positives. An example of an over-constrained assumption is shown in Fig. 3. The assertion requires the read data (PRDATA) to remain stable when it is still not ready (!PREADY), which is not a necessary constraint. However, the assumption above accidentally removes all wait states (assuming PRDATA will always be ready), thereby passing the incorrect assertion. 3) Partly-implemented RTL designs: An RTL design, even being golden, may only implement a subset of behaviors allowed by a specification. An assertion that violates the specification may still pass on a valid RTL implementation if the RTL does not choose to implement that part of the specification. For example, Fig. 4a demonstrates an incorrect property about when the design can leave a denial state (indicated by QDENY). However, since the RTL design never enters the denial state (which is a valid implementation for the specification), the assertion will pass trivially.

B. Coverage Analysis to Evaluate Completeness

However, while coverage analysis is helpful in assisting thorough design verification, it does not directly measure how well the SVA properties capture the requirements in the specification documents. Various coverage analysis techniques exist, each providing different trade-offs between accuracy and computational cost. Without loss of generality, we discuss two techniques supported by JasperGold [21], a widely used industrial formal verification platform. 1) Cone-of-influence (COI) Analysis: This method performs structural analysis to identify all design signals and logic elements within the fan-in cone of the assertions. Though computationally inexpensive, this metric is very inaccurate. For example, tautologies contribute to COI coverage. An LLM which generates tautologies that include all design signals can achieve 100% COI coverage despite being totally useless. 2) Proof Core Analysis: This method leverages model checking to identify the subset of design logic that is required to prove an assertion. The resulting proof core represents the minimal or near-minimal portion of the design necessary to establish correctness, making it more accurate than COI analysis. However, the dependence on model checking also leads to its own sources of inaccuracies: (1) the assumptions do not contribute to coverage since their proof core cannot be computed; (2) the RTL design may only implement a subset of specified design behaviors. For example, the assertion in Fig. 4b is correct and useful with respect to the specification,

III. SVAEVAL EVALUATION METHODOLOGIES

This section describes the methods and algorithms of SVAEVAL. We consider two scenarios: If a golden SVA property set is provided (scenario 1), the SVAEVAL-FORMAL framework is used to formally evaluate any test property sets; Without golden SVA property sets (scenario 2), the SVAEVAL-HYBRID framework combines formal and LLMbased techniques to compare different test property sets.

A. Scenario 1: With Golden SVA Property Sets

A golden SVA property set, denoted G = {g1, g2, ..., gm}, is a formal specification that defines all valid execution traces of the design. That is,

τ ∈T is valid ⇔∀g ∈G, τ |= g

where T denotes the set of all possible traces over the set of signals from the specification. Given the golden property set, we can formally evaluate the correctness, completeness, and usefulness of any LLMgenerated property set (T = {t1, t2, ..., tn}).

• Correctness: A property t ∈T is incorrect, or overconstrained, if there exists a valid execution trace of the design that violates the property. That is,

t is incorrect in T ⇔∃τ ∈T , τ |= G ∧τ ̸|= t,

where τ |= G is a short-hand for ∀g ∈G, τ |= g.

• Completeness: T is complete if and only if it eliminates all invalid design behaviors. This means that every valid trace of T should also be a valid trace of G. Therefore, if a valid trace of T violates any property g ∈G, then T is incomplete, and g is a missing property in T:

g is missing in T ⇔∃τ ∈T , τ |= T ∧τ ̸|= g.

• Usefulness: We say a property t is useless, or redundant, if it does not add new constraints to the set. That is, any trace that satisfies T \ {t} also satisfies t:

t is redundant in T ⇔∀τ ∈T , τ |= T \ {t} ⇒τ |= t.

A special category of useless properties is tautology, where the property is satisfied by any possible trace:

t is a tautology ⇔∀τ ∈T , τ |= t.

We implement the above checks with a model checker, where T is represented as a free unconstrained model over symbolic inputs, i.e., it can produce all possible sequences of signal values in the specification. We use JasperGold (version 2021.03) [21] as the model checker in our experiments. We develop iterative algorithms that use these checks to identify incorrect, missing, tautological, and redundant properties from the LLM-generated property sets. For example,

Algorithm 1 computes a minimal irredundant set from the target set. The other algorithms are implemented similarly. The evaluation flow of SVAEVAL-FORMAL is demonstrated in Fig. 5. To obtain accurate results, the correctness check should precede completeness and redundancy checks. Otherwise, incorrect properties in T might cause the following checks to (1) fail to detect missing properties and (2) mark irredundant properties as redundant. For example, consider the extreme case where an LLM generated the property assert 1’b0 in T. Since no execution trace satisfies this property, it can be seen from the above equations that (1) none of the properties in G would be marked as missing, and (2) all other properties in T would be marked as redundant. Therefore, all incorrect (over-constrained) properties should be removed before the completeness and redundancy checks. The tautology check is independent of the others. We run it first simply because it is fast and reduces the input size for other algorithms. Ideally, a golden property set should correctly and completely reflect the intent of its natural language specification and should contain no useless properties. For complex design protocols, however, it is difficult to ensure that a property set is complete with respect to the entire specification. Fortunately, a human-generated property set doesn’t have to be complete for the evaluation to be accurate. Instead, the correctness check will remain accurate as long as the humangenerated set, denoted G′, satisfies the following conditions: (1) Every property in G′ is correct. This ensures that any incorrect property in T is detected. (2) G′ is more complete than any test property set T it compares to, i.e., any property t ∈T, if correct, should also be covered by G′. This will

prevent correct properties in T from being marked incorrect. With these two conditions satisfied, the SVAEVAL-FORMAL evaluation flow remains accurate, except that the completeness check only shows missing properties from G′ instead of G. In practice, the second condition can be ensured by manually inspecting the properties marked incorrect after the correctness check. If all of these properties are indeed incorrect, then the condition is satisfied. Otherwise, the user can improve the completeness of the golden property set, by simply adding the marked properties that are determined to be correct, and relaunch the evaluation flow. This refinement process is optional and only needed when the user is unsure whether the golden property set is complete.

B. Scenario 2: Without Golden SVA Property Sets

Without a golden SVA property set, the only ground truth for evaluating the correctness and completeness of a test property set is the informal specification document. While it is common to use LLM-as-a-judge [22] in such a setting, relying solely on LLMs can lead to unreliable assessments. In particular, when the LLMs used by the SVA generator and the judge possess similar reasoning limitations, the judge may fail to identify incorrect or incomplete properties from the generated SVA property sets, thereby reducing the reliability of the evaluation process. We propose SVAEVAL-HYBRID, a hybrid formal and LLMbased approach that compares the relative correctness and completeness of two test property sets, allowing us to compare different SVA generators. The comparison algorithm is shown in Fig. 6. 1) Identifying Unique Properties: A property t in Test Set 1 (T1) is unique with respect to Test Set 2 (T2) if it creates additional constraints when added to T2. That is, there exists a valid execution trace of T2 that violates t:

is unique(t, T2) ⇔∃τ ∈T , τ |= T2 ∧τ ̸|= t.

This check is used to identify unique properties from both property sets. Note that these unique properties are where the two SVA generators disagree with each other, and it is not clear if each of them is correct or incorrect. 2) CEX-supported LLM-based Correctness Check: When the model checker identifies a unique property t, it also provides the corresponding counterexample (CEX) trace τ. This CEX is used by an Evaluation LLM (effectively serving as an LLM-judge) in conjunction with the design documents to help determine the correctness of the property. If the CEX is a valid execution trace of the design, then the unique property, which it violates, is deemed to be incorrect. If the CEX is invalid, then it increases the confidence that the property is correct. In the absence of a formal ground truth, at some point we will need to rely on an LLM-judge. Providing the LLMjudge with a CEX increases its overall success as compared to providing the property alone. 3) Iterative Comparison: After removing incorrect properties, the formal method may identify new unique properties.

Therefore, we repeat the process until no new unique properties are identified. Note that this algorithm compares the relative correctness and completeness of the two property sets. If the two sets (1) contain the same incorrect property or (2) miss the same necessary property, the algorithm does not detect it. The evaluation flow of SVAEVAL-HYBRID is demonstrated in Fig. 7. The comparison algorithm replaces the correctness and completeness checks in SVAEVAL-FORMAL, determining the (1) uniquely incorrect and (2) uniquely correct properties from both test sets. A combined property set is formed by removing the uniquely incorrect properties, which improves the correctness and completeness from both property sets. We discuss the inaccuracies of the comparison algorithm that are intrinsic to the lack of a formal ground-truth and intrinsic to the overall dependence of LLMs for automation. First, since the shared incorrect properties cannot be detected by the formal methods, they will remain in the combined property check. However, this does not affect the accuracy in comparing the relative correctness and completeness of the two sets. In contrast, incorrect LLM decisions affect both the comparison and the combined property set. These include (1) false positives, where uniquely incorrect properties are categorized as correct and put into the combined set; and (2) false negatives, where uniquely correct properties are categorized as incorrect and discarded. The redundancy check is also affected by previous inaccuracies in the comparison algorithm. Specifically, if incorrect properties are undetected and remain in the set, they may cause other correct properties to appear redundant. This is why we do not remove redundancy in the final combined property set. We don’t want to risk removing correct and useful properties. On

IV. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS

To demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed evaluation methodologies, we selected 4 hardware protocols [23]– [26] as our test cases, as shown in Table I. Existing opensource works have developed formal specifications for these protocols [12], [20]. Building upon these efforts, we carefully construct golden property sets that correctly and completely reflect their design specification documents. Compared with the other test cases, AXI is substantially more complex due to its multiple independent channels, support for outstanding and out-of-order transactions, burst transfers, and numerous optional features. Therefore, our manually created property set is not complete (compared to the AMBA 3 AXI Protocol Checker User Guide released by ARM [27]). We mitigate this by removing several sections in the specification document that explain certain features (cache support, protection unit support, and atomic accesses), thereby focusing on a well-defined subset of the protocol. Moreover, we ensure that our golden property set is more complete than any test set by manually inspecting the result of the correctness check, as discussed in Section III-A, to ensure the accuracy of the SVAEVAL-FORMAL framework. To compare SVAEVAL with previous RTL-implementationbased evaluation methods, we obtain 3 open-source RTL designs that implement these protocols. The WISHBONE DMA/Bridge IP Core (wb_dma), obtained from Open- Cores [28], provides DMA transfers between two WISHBONE interfaces, each containing a master and slave. The core is extended with the Q-Channel low-power interface and used as a test case in an EDA project [29]. The APB and AXI RAM modules (apb_ram, axi_ram) are obtained from the Taxi Transport Library [30]. We evaluate various SVA generation techniques, using different models, as shown in columns 1-2 of Table II:

• Zero-shot prompting: Our baseline method uses a simple prompt in a zero-shot setting to ask LLMs to generate SVA properties from design specifications. To compare LLMs with different reasoning capabilities, we select the frontier GPT-5.4 model and the deprecated GPT-4o model in our experiments.

• Multi-stage SVA generation: Numerous end-to-end frameworks decompose SVA generation into multiple tasks, each targeted by specialized LLMs [11], [13]– [17]. We select SANGAM [15], one of the state-of-the-art

among these frameworks. SANGAM consists of 3 main steps: (1) Specification Processing, which uses 3 LLMs to extract signal-wise information from the document; (2) Assertion Reasoning, using a Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)-based algorithm to expand and fix the property sets based on feedback from both LLMs and the Cadence JasperGold Formal Verification tool [21]; and (3) Assertion Combination, a final stage that de-duplicates all generated properties with an LLM to produce the final set. Again, we run the SANGAM framework with GPT-5.4 and GPT-4o in our experiments.

• Fine-tuning LLMs for NL-to-SVA translation: Recent works have also fine-tuned LLMs to improve sentencelevel NL-to-SVA translation [9], [31]. For example, QiMeng-CodeV-SVA [9] provided an NL-SVA dataset with 83K instances, and fine-tuned open-source models into CodeV-SVA, a series of models specialized for NLto-SVA translation. They also applied CodeV-SVA to an end-to-end SVA generation framework [32], replacing the LLM used in the NL-to-SVA stage with CodeV- SVA, demonstrating an increased number of syntactically correct and FPV passed assertions. Our SANGAM+QiMeng setting uses the SANGAM framework but replaces the NL-to-SVA model with Qwen3-8B and its fine-tuned CodeV-SVA-8B, to evaluate the effectiveness of this method.

A. Scenario 1: With Golden SVA Property Sets

We apply the SVAEVAL-FORMAL framework to evaluate each generated SVA property set against the golden set of the corresponding test case. The results are shown in Table II. Column 3 (Total) shows the total number of generated properties, combining all 4 test cases, for each SVA generator. Column 4 (Inc-syntax) shows the number of properties with syntax errors. Columns 5-7 show the number of functionally incorrect (Inc-function), tautological (Tautology), and redundant (Redundant) properties detected by the SVAEVAL- FORMAL framework. Column 8 (Useful) shows the remaining useful properties. We also compute the percentage of each category, divided by the total number of generated properties. Finally, column 9 (Missing) shows the number of missing properties identified by SVAEVAL-FORMAL, divided by the number of human-expert-generated golden properties. Our experiments demonstrate that, despite recent advances, current LLM-based SVA generators remain far from matching human experts in generating high-quality SVA properties from specification documents. For example, none of the SVA generators exceeds 60% correctness. In terms of completeness, the best SVA generator captures less than 70% of the properties in our manually developed property sets. Detailed discussions on the effectiveness and remaining challenges of recent SVA generators are provided in Section V.

B. Scenario 2: Without Golden SVA Property Sets

In Section III-B, we propose SVAEVAL-HYBRID to compare different SVA generators even without human-expertgenerated golden property sets. We now evaluate the effectiveness of this methodology by using the golden property sets as Test Set 2 in Fig. 7, which gives us ground truth to evaluate each of the steps in this methodology. We would like to emphasize that in this setting, the methodology is not aware that Test Set 2 is the golden set. This information is known only to us to help understand the quality of the results produced by the methodology. The results are shown in Table III. Instead of just evaluating one test set, each comparison now includes metrics for both property sets. The Inc-function column now records the uniquely incorrect properties; the Additional column, replacing Missing, records the uniquely correct properties. The syntax and tautology checks are not affected and are as accurate as those in SVAEVAL-FORMAL. Given that Test Set 2 is the golden set, SVAEVAL-HYBRID should report the same number of Inc-function as in SVAEVAL-FORMAL for the SVA generators (T1), while the manual set (T2) should have 0 functional errors; the same applies for Redundant; for Additional, the SVA generators (T1) should have 0 additional properties, while the additional properties of the manual sets (T2) are the missing properties in SVAEVAL- FORMAL. Inaccuracies arise since SVAEVAL-HYBRID has an LLM-based comparison, while SVAEVAL-FORMAL only uses formal checks. While there are some inaccuracies, SVAEVAL-HYBRID is able to show that the LLM-based SVA generators (T1) have much lower correctness rates, much lower usefulness rates, and less additional properties than T2, demonstrating the superiority of human experts, just like SVAEVAL-FORMAL. This demonstrates the effectiveness of our evaluation approach in comparing different SVA generators, even without the need for golden property sets. The only exception is SANGAM GPT- 5.4, where SVAEVAL-HYBRID mistakenly reports that the SVA generator has more additional properties. Table IV shows the error rate of our framework. As discussed in Section III-B, false positives (FP) result from categorizing uniquely incorrect properties as additional (uniquely correct), and similarly for false negatives (FN). The errors are divided by the total number of properties from both sets. Our comparison framework achieves an average error rate of 9.48% across the 6 SVA generators. The framework is more

accurate when evaluating weaker models (GPT-4o and Qwen3- 8B), with an average error rate of 4.56%. In contrast, the average error rate when evaluating stronger models (GPT-5.4 and CodeV-SVA-8B) is 14.4%. These errors come mainly from higher false positives rates. This is because the SVA generators have reached capabilities similar to the Evaluation LLM (GPT- 5.4). Therefore, the errors in the models are subtle enough to mislead the Evaluation LLM.

C. RTL-Implementation-based Evaluation Methods

We also assess the RTL-implementation-based evaluation methods, including model checking and coverage analysis, on all the SVA property sets in our experiments. As shown in Tables V and VI, LLM-based SVA generators often generate more passed assertions, comparable assertion pass rates, and even comparable or higher coverages, compared to manually-developed SVA property sets. However, these results from RTL-implementation-based evaluations are not accurate: SVAEVAL shows that none of the SVA generators comes even close to the manually-developed SVA property sets from human experts in both correctness and completeness.

B. Multi-stage (SANGAM) vs monolithic (baseline)

Although SANGAM generates substantially more properties than baseline, the improvement in completeness is relatively limited. For example, with GPT-5.4, SANGAM achieves a 13.6x increase in total property count. Even after removing the incorrect properties, it still has 12.9x more properties. However, it only covers 5 more properties in the manual sets. The reason is that a significant portion of the properties generated by SANGAM are tautological or redundant. In particular, since SANGAM instructs an LLM to extract per-signal information from the specification, the LLM ends up extracting the same properties for multiple signals. Using Fig. 4b as an example, the same property will be extracted for all QREQn, QACCEPTn and QDENY. Interestingly, SANGAM seems to provide more improvements over baseline when using weaker models. For GPT- 4o, the framework reduces error rates by 20.08% and covers 10.58% more properties in the manual sets, suggesting that decomposition and iterative refinement compensate for the

weaker reasoning capability of the older model. In contrast, for GPT-5.4, the monolithic approach already achieves relatively strong performance, while the multi-stage processing barely improves correctness and completeness, and creates a lot of tautology and redundancy. This observation suggests that some frameworks developed for older LLMs may become less beneficial as frontier models improve in information retrieval and reasoning capabilities.

C. Fine-tuning LLMs for NL-to-SVA translation

Replacing the NL-to-SVA translation task from Qwen3-8B to the fine-tuned CodeV-SVA-8B model reduces error rate by 6.04%, indicating a better NL-to-SVA translation capability. These findings are consistent with previous observations in QiMeng-CodeV-SVA [9], which reported improvements in both syntactically correct and FPV-passed assertions. Moreover, the number of missing properties also reduces from 94.12% to 83.53%, indicating that a more proper NL-to-SVA translation indeed results in improving the completeness of the end-to-end framework.

Finally, current LLMs still struggle to generate properties for complex design behaviors. For example, the AXI protocol specifies sophisticated rules governing burst transfers, interchannel dependencies, and transaction ordering. Verifying these behaviors often requires auxiliary SystemVerilog logic to maintain and correlate transaction state across multiple cycles. In our experiments, current LLM-based SVA generators frequently fail to synthesize such auxiliary logic correctly, resulting in functionally incorrect properties. These challenges remain largely unexplored in current SVA generation research. Dealing with ambiguous text or inconsistent information would require cross-document reasoning over heterogeneous specification artifacts. Rather than generating properties from isolated textual snippets, future frameworks should jointly analyze natural language descriptions, timing diagrams, and any form of relevant information throughout the specification to infer the intended behavior. VI. LIMITATIONS

Dependence on formal semantics. Our evaluation methodology is fundamentally based on formal verification and symbolic model checking. As a result, our framework also inherits the limitations of formal verification tools. For example, hardware description languages such as SystemVerilog are naturally expressed using four-state logic (0/1/X/Z). In simulation-based verification, unknown (X) and high-impedance (Z) values are explicitly represented and often play an important role in RTL debugging. In contrast, formal verification tools generally interpret X and Z as unconstrained symbolic choices in two-state (0/1) logic. Consequently, properties that explicitly depend on four-state logic may not be meaningfully evaluated in our framework. For example, the $isunknown(<signal>) construct is typically reduced to false during formal analysis. We exclude any properties that contain simulation-oriented semantics from our experiments. Dependence on Specification Documents. Our methodology assumes that all the intended design behaviors are described in available specification documents. However, in industrial practice, specifications are often incomplete or even absent, especially for emerging designs. Even for designs implementing standardized protocols, specification documents typically describe only architectural behavior. RTL designs frequently contain micro-architectural optimizations for performance and power concerns, which will not be captured by the architecture-level specifications. As a consequence, verification engineers sometimes work with the RTL design itself, with little or no reference from specification documents, to develop SVA properties. Recent research has also explored this direction, developing LLM-based techniques to generate SVA properties from both specifications and RTL designs [31]–[41], or even from RTL designs alone [42]–[44]. Similarly, current works rely on the inaccurate implementation-based methods to evaluate the generated SVA properties. Developing reliable evaluation methodologies for RTL-centric SVA generation requires entirely different mindsets, and remains an important direction for future research.

VII. RELATED WORK

NL2SVA evaluation methods. Recent works have proposed benchmarks that translate high-level NL description to SVA properties (NL2SVA). FVEval [45] constructed both realworld and synthetic benchmarks to evaluate the ability of various LLMs in generating syntactically and functionally correct SVA properties. Hybrid-NL2SVA [31] and QiMeng-CodeV- SVA [9] focused on developing high-quality benchmarks to

fine-tune open-source models. Hybrid-NL2SVA collected 4K SVAs from hardware verification textbooks; QiMeng-CodeV- SVA used LLMs to generate NL-SVA pairs from RTL code and performs distillation to obtain 83K instances. To evaluate functional correctness, these works utilize formal verification tools to check the exact logical equivalence between a pair of model-generated and ground-truth properties. In contrast, our work focuses on evaluating end-to-end SVA generation from design specification documents. SVAEVAL compares the correctness, completeness, and usefulness of entire SVA property sets. Assessing importance of individual properties. Beyond correctness, recent work has also explored estimating the relative importance of individual properties. Spec2Assertion [14] proposes an importance score computed using signal dependency graphs extracted from RTL designs, where properties spanning longer dependency paths are assigned higher scores. This approach is complementary to ours and can be applied to evaluate different aspects of a generated SVA property set.

VIII. CONCLUSIONS AND FUTURE DIRECTIONS

We present SVAEVAL, an evaluation framework for LLMbased SVA generators, which operates under two scenarios: (1) With golden SVA property sets developed by human experts, SVAEVAL-FORMAL implements a formal framework to evaluate the correctness, completeness and usefulness of generated SVA property sets; (2) Without golden SVA property sets, SVAEVAL-HYBRID implements a hybrid formal and LLM-based framework to compare different generated SVA property sets. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of SVAEVAL over existing RTL-implementationbased evaluation methods. Based on the results, we analyze the effectiveness of various SVA generation techniques and discuss remaining challenges. Currently, our evaluation dataset remains relatively small due to the significant effort required for manual construction and validation. As LLM-based SVA generators continue to improve, larger and more diverse benchmarks will become increasingly important for reliable evaluation. Recent research in a software security has explored using a reliable comparison framework to help revising formal specifications [46]. For SVA generation, SVAEVAL-HYBRID provides a promising direction towards this goal, since it enables the combination of SVA property sets from multiple generators into progressively improved property sets without requiring exhaustive manual inspection. For future work, we plan to leverage this framework to construct a continuously expanding and progressively improving dataset for future research on automated SVA generation and evaluation.
